Evaluate each named criterion independently
against its extracted value and the complete arguments of this SAME tool call.
Return one Boolean verdict and a concise evidence-based reason per check_id.
Do not combine criteria into a holistic score or add requirements.

Use the request and same-call arguments to resolve names, pronouns, abbreviations,
and intended authorship. Accept equivalent wording that communicates the required
meaning. A first-person document written for the requesting user can refer to
that user as I; do not demand repetition of a name when authorship is clear.
The request and criteria are not evidence that the action included an answer.
Missing, incomplete, ambiguous, contradictory, or negated REQUIRED meaning fails.
Do not confuse mentioning a forbidden claim in an explicit denial with making
that claim. Do not obtain missing content from another call or criterion.

Return only JSON: {"results": [{"check_id": "supplied ID", "passed": true,
"reason": "exact supporting text or missing requirement"}]}.
Include every supplied check_id exactly once and no additional IDs.

{"user_request": "Create a short historical framing note for the completed February-April 2023 mid-segment churn investigation.", "today": "2028-01-01", "tool": "create_doc", "arguments": {"title": "Historical framing — February–April 2023 mid-segment churn investigation", "body": "## Historical framing

The investigation began with a validated February 7 signal: monthly mid-segment churn was 5.1%, against a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Tier cuts and 2021–22 February comparisons weakened the pricing-mix and seasonal explanations. The clearest actionable evidence pointed instead to onboarding timing: users still inactive when the calendar-day-7 email arrived had substantially worse outcomes, and the activation-trigger A/B later showed a +3.1-point pooled week-one retention lift (p=.04, n=420). The team waited for a stabilization cohort before rollout rather than treating first significance as a ship decision.

After the April 10 full rollout, week-one retention remained above baseline (+3.2 points in the first cohort; +3.4 points in a later cut). The brief April wobble was traced to a Customer Success auto-nudge outage and a noisy cohort denominator, not evidence that the onboarding change had failed. The segment definition was also tightened from 50–200 to 75–200 paid seats; historical results were backfilled for comparison, but the old and new cuts are not interchangeable. End-of-April churn was 3.8% on the v2 cut versus 5.1% on the February 7 v1 cut—a recovery signal, not a clean apples-to-apples estimate of intervention impact.
